title: Asian Cup Organisers Say Saudi Tournament Still On Despite Attacks
excerpt: The 2027 Asian Cup remains set for January 7-February 5 in Saudi Arabia, organisers say, while golf, cycling, tennis and esports events in the kingdom are postponed or cancelled after the Riyadh airport attack.
body:
• The 2027 Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia remains scheduled for January 7 to February 5, local organisers said on Friday, across eight stadiums in Riyadh, Jeddah and Al Khobar.
  • Golf's $5 million Saudi International, due November 18-21 in Riyadh, has been postponed indefinitely, and the Urban Cycling World Championships scheduled for November 3-7 have been cancelled.
  • The decisions follow a Houthi-claimed strike on Riyadh's international airport last Saturday that killed at least 12 people and wounded more than 300, according to Reuters.
  • The Asian Football Confederation has not ruled out a move to 2028, with its president saying it is in no hurry to decide and will assess the situation through the end of November.

The Asian Cup football tournament will go ahead in Saudi Arabia early next year on its original schedule, local organisers said, even as a series of attacks on Riyadh forced the postponement or cancellation of other major sporting events in the kingdom.

The statement from the tournament's Local Organising Committee (LOC), reported by Reuters, came after days of disruption that raised questions about whether the 24-team continental championship could still be staged from January 7 to February 5, 2027.

"Preparations across all organisational and operational areas are progressing according to the approved schedule, including work on venues, facilities and supporting services."

— Asian Cup Local Organising Committee

The committee added that it would continue to monitor developments and ensure the appropriate conditions were in place for the tournament's successful delivery. The competition, being staged in Saudi Arabia for the first time, is due to use eight stadiums in Riyadh, Jeddah and Al Khobar, according to Inside World Football.

The attack that disrupted the calendar

Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi movement claimed responsibility for Saturday's strike on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport, which killed at least 12 people and wounded more than 300. Reuters described it as the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade. Other attacks in recent days have targeted aviation and oil infrastructure, and the airport has faced an extended shutdown and significant flight disruption.

Golf, cycling, tennis and esports all move

Golf's Asian Tour postponed the Saudi International indefinitely. The $5 million event, sponsored by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF) and described as the flagship tournament on the tour, was due at Riyadh Golf Club from November 18 to 21.

"The decision to postpone was taken following an assessment of the organisational and logistical challenges associated with hosting the tournament and ensuring the event is delivered to a standard befitting its international stature."

— Asian Tour

The Urban Cycling World Championships, scheduled for November 3 to 7 in Riyadh and featuring trials and BMX Freestyle, were cancelled. The UCI said the decision followed a joint assessment of recent developments and their impact on logistics. Australia had already withdrawn its team, with AusCycling saying the safety and wellbeing of athletes and staff was its highest priority.

The Six Kings Slam exhibition tennis tournament in Riyadh has been moved from October to December, FIFA has postponed the FIFAe Finals 2026 video game competition in Jeddah until an unspecified future date, and three Saudi Pro League fixtures were shifted because of logistical concerns, as SuperSport reported in its coverage of the golf postponement.

Why the Asian Cup decision is different

The Asian Cup has more time, and more at stake. Saudi Arabia pitched the tournament as an early rehearsal for hosting the FIFA World Cup in 2034, the centrepiece of a heavy programme of sports investment through the PIF in recent years. Cancelling or moving a continental championship involving 24 national teams would be a far larger step than postponing a golf tournament or an exhibition tennis event.

That does not mean the January dates are guaranteed. Asian Football Confederation president Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa said earlier this week that a postponement until 2028 was possible if necessary. Inside World Football reported that the AFC is taking a wait-and-see approach, that Al Khalifa said the confederation was in no hurry to make a decision, and that the situation would be assessed through to the end of November. Football Australia and the Korea Football Association are among the federations closely monitoring developments.

What happens next

If attacks stop and flights through Riyadh normalise, the LOC's schedule can hold. If they continue into November, the AFC will have to weigh those assurances against the safety concerns already acted on by other organisers. No new dates, venues or ticket guidance have been announced.
